lead: A derivative is a new function. At each input x it returns the slope of the graph of f at that point, or the instantaneous rate of change of f. It exists only when the limit of a difference quotient exists. This idea turns a curve into a slope machine: speed from distance, marginal cost from total cost, and a tangent line from a graph. Engineers use it to find best values of settings, and analysts use it to read rates in data.
prereq: You need function notation and graphs from Chapter 1.1 and limits and continuity from Chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: Fix a point x. Move a small distance h to x+h. The average slope between the two points on y=f(x) is the difference quotient. It is rise divided by run:

blocks.where: Q(h) is the average slope over [x, x+h]; h is a nonzero change in input; f(x+h)−f(x) is the change in output.

blocks.text: Let h shrink toward 0. If Q(h) has a limit, that limit is the derivative at x and is written f′(x). The derivative as a function assigns this value to every x where the limit exists.

blocks.where: f′(x) is the derivative function; x is an input in its domain; h is the input change tending to 0.

blocks.text: Other notation: y′ and dy/dx. In dy/dx, dy and dx are not separate ordinary numbers; the symbol means the same limit, read as the derivative of y with respect to x. The value at a single point a is f′(a), a number. As x varies, f′(x) is a new function. The tangent at a is y−f(a)=f′(a)(x−a).

A function is differentiable at a if f′(a) exists. It is differentiable on an interval if it is differentiable at every point of the interval. Differentiability is local: it depends on behaviour close to a.
If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a. Reason: write f(a+h)−f(a)=([f(a+h)−f(a)]/h)h. As h→0, the bracket tends to f′(a) and h tends to 0, so f(a+h)→f(a).

The converse fails. The absolute value f(x)=|x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there. For h>0, [|0+h|−|0|]/h=h/h=1. For h<0, it is (−h)/h=−1. The left and right limits differ, so the limit does not exist. The graph has a corner at x=0.

A cusp is a sharper corner where slopes run to opposite infinities; y=x<sup>2/3</sup> at x=0 is one. A jump, a hole, or a vertical tangent also blocks a finite derivative. A function can be continuous everywhere yet fail at one point. For two or three variables, differentiability is stronger and needs a linear approximation; see Unit 4, Functions of Several Variables.
For common functions, use standard rules instead of the limit each time. Let c be a constant, n a real number, and u, v differentiable functions of x.

The chain rule is the workhorse. Differentiate the outer function at the inner value, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function. For y=(3x²+1)<sup>5</sup>, dy/dx=5(3x²+1)<sup>4</sup>·6x=30x(3x²+1)<sup>4</sup>. The derivative function may have a smaller domain than f because points with corners or vertical tangents are removed.

items: At a point a, the tangent slope is f′(a).
The normal line is perpendicular to the tangent, with slope −1/f′(a) when f′(a)≠0.
Higher derivatives come by differentiating again: f″ is the derivative of f′. For example, the derivative of x<sup>3</sup> is 3x<sup>2</sup>, and its second derivative is 6x.

figure.caption: The curve is y=x². The line y=6x−9 is the tangent at x=3; it touches at (3,9), where the slope is 6.

spec.aria: The blue tangent line y equals 6x minus 9 touches the grey parabola y equals x squared at x equals 3.

examples.question: For f(x)=x², use the difference quotient to find f′(3). Then write the tangent line at x=3.
steps: At x=3, form Q(h)=[f(3+h)−f(3)]/h with h≠0.
Divide by h: Q(h)=6+h for h≠0.
Let h→0: f′(3)=lim<sub>h→0</sub>(6+h)=6. The slope at x=3 is 6.
examples.answer: f′(3)=6, and the tangent at x=3 is y=6x−9, touching the curve at (3,9).
examples.check:
x0 = 3
h = 1e-6
f = lambda x: x*x
slope = (f(x0+h)-f(x0))/h
m = round(slope)
c = round(f(x0) - m*x0)
y0 = round(f(x0))
print(m)
print(c)
print(y0)

traps: Differentiable implies continuous, not the reverse: |x| at 0 is continuous but has no derivative.
f′(a) is a number at one point; f′(x) is a function. Do not mix the value with the rule.
dy/dx is one symbol, not a fraction of two ordinary numbers; do not cancel dx.
A corner or cusp gives no derivative; a vertical tangent also gives no finite derivative.
In the chain rule, multiply by the inner derivative; leaving out g′(x) is the commonest error.

quiz.q: State the limit definition of f′(a).
Explain why differentiability at a implies continuity at a.
quiz.a: Write f(a+h)−f(a)=([f(a+h)−f(a)]/h)h. The bracket tends to f′(a) and h tends to 0, so f(a+h)→f(a).

quiz.q: Discuss differentiability of f(x)=|x−2| at x=2.
quiz.a: f is continuous at 2. For h>0 the quotient is 1; for h<0 it is −1. The one-sided limits differ, so f′(2) does not exist.

quiz.q: Give one difference between f′(a) and f′(x).
quiz.a: f′(a) is the slope at the single input a. f′(x) is the rule that gives the slope at every x where the derivative exists.

quiz.q: Give a function that is continuous at 0 but not differentiable at 0, and justify with one-sided limits.
quiz.a: f(x)=|x|. The right quotient is 1 and the left quotient is −1; the two limits differ, so f′(0) does not exist.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software computes derivatives symbolically or by automatic differentiation, which applies the chain rule to code. Numerical differentiation estimates f′(x) with a small h but suffers rounding error. In machine learning, gradients of loss functions are derivatives with many inputs; see Unit 4. Search terms: automatic differentiation, finite difference, gradient descent.
